stem: The gas that makes up the largest proportion (about 78%) of the Earth's atmosphere by volume is:
solution: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the Earth's atmosphere, making up about 78% (roughly 78.08%) of the dry air by volume. Oxygen is the second most abundant, at about 21% (20.95%). Nitrogen is important as it dilutes oxygen (preventing rapid burning), and it is essential for living organisms (plants need nitrogen compounds, and nitrogen is 'fixed' from the air into the soil). Understanding that nitrogen (~78%) is the most abundant atmospheric gas is a fundamental prelims point. Nitrogen (~78%) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere.

stem: Oxygen makes up approximately what proportion of the atmosphere by volume?
solution: Oxygen makes up approximately 21% (about 20.95%) of the Earth's atmosphere by volume — the second most abundant gas after nitrogen (~78%). Oxygen is essential for the respiration of living organisms and for combustion (burning). Together, nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%) make up about 99% of the atmosphere; the remaining ~1% is argon, carbon dioxide, and other trace gases. Understanding that oxygen is ~21% of the atmosphere is a fundamental prelims point. Oxygen makes up about 21% of the atmosphere.

stem: After nitrogen and oxygen, the next most abundant gas in the atmosphere (about 0.93%) is:
solution: After nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%), the next most abundant gas in the atmosphere is argon, an inert (noble) gas, which makes up about 0.93% of the air by volume. Carbon dioxide, though very important climatically, is present in a much smaller proportion (about 0.03–0.04%). So the order of the three most abundant gases is nitrogen > oxygen > argon. Understanding that argon (~0.93%) is the third most abundant atmospheric gas is a prelims point. Argon (~0.93%) is the third most abundant gas in the atmosphere.

stem: Carbon dioxide (CO2) makes up only about __________ of the atmosphere, yet it is very important because it is a greenhouse gas and is used by plants in photosynthesis.
solution: Carbon dioxide (CO2) makes up only about 0.03% (roughly 0.03–0.04%) of the atmosphere by volume — a very small fraction. Despite this tiny proportion, CO2 is very important: it is a greenhouse gas (it absorbs and re-radiates heat/outgoing terrestrial radiation, warming the atmosphere — the 'greenhouse effect'), and it is essential for plants, which use it (along with water and sunlight) in photosynthesis to make food. The concentration of CO2 has been rising due to human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation), contributing to global warming. Understanding that CO2 is only ~0.03% but is a crucial greenhouse gas is a prelims point. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.03% of the atmosphere but is an important greenhouse gas.

stem: Which gas, though present only in tiny amounts, is important because it absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun in the stratosphere?
solution: Ozone (O3) is a gas present only in tiny amounts (in trace quantities) in the atmosphere, but it is extremely important because, in the stratosphere (where it is concentrated, in the 'ozone layer'), it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation coming from the Sun, protecting life on Earth from the damaging effects of excessive UV rays (which can cause skin cancer, harm to eyes, and damage to plants and marine life). Ozone is found mainly in the stratosphere (at heights of roughly 10–50 km). Understanding that ozone absorbs harmful UV radiation is a prelims point. Ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, protecting life on Earth.

stem: The 'ozone layer', which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, is located mainly in which layer of the atmosphere?
solution: The ozone layer — the region of concentrated ozone (O3) that absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation — is located mainly in the stratosphere, the second layer of the atmosphere (roughly 10/13 km to 50 km altitude). Ozone is concentrated at heights of about 10 to 50 km (with maximum concentration around 20–30 km), within the stratosphere. Because the ozone layer absorbs UV radiation (and this warms the stratosphere), temperature actually increases with height in the stratosphere. Understanding that the ozone layer lies in the stratosphere is a key prelims point. The ozone layer is located in the stratosphere.

stem: Water vapour in the atmosphere is important because:
options: It is a fixed, unchanging component everywhere
It is the source of all precipitation (rain, snow), it is a greenhouse gas, and its amount varies from place to place
It has no effect on weather
It is only found above 50 km
solution: Water vapour — water in its gaseous (invisible) form — is a very important variable component of the atmosphere. It is important because: it is the source of all forms of precipitation (rain, snow, hail, etc.) and of clouds and fog (when it condenses); it is a powerful greenhouse gas (it absorbs both incoming solar and outgoing terrestrial radiation, regulating the air temperature); and its amount is highly variable — it varies greatly from place to place and time to time (from almost nil over deserts and cold poles to as much as ~4% over warm, wet tropical/oceanic areas — decreasing from the equator toward the poles, and from the surface upward). Because it is so variable, water vapour is not listed among the fixed proportions of the permanent gases. Understanding the importance and variability of water vapour is a prelims point. Water vapour is a variable greenhouse gas and the source of all precipitation.

stem: The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere generally __________ from the equator towards the poles.
solution: The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere generally decreases from the equator towards the poles. This is because water vapour comes from the evaporation of water, which is greater where it is warm and where there is plentiful water (as in the warm, humid tropics near the equator), and much less where it is cold (as near the poles, where cold air holds little moisture). So water vapour is greatest over the warm equatorial regions and decreases poleward (it also decreases with altitude, upward from the surface). Understanding this latitudinal decrease of water vapour is a prelims point. Water vapour decreases from the equator towards the poles.

stem: Tiny solid particles (like dust, pollen, soot, salt, and smoke) suspended in the atmosphere are important because they:
options: Act as surfaces (hygroscopic nuclei) on which water vapour condenses to form clouds, and they scatter/reflect sunlight (affecting sky colour)
Are found only at the poles
solution: Tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere — such as dust, pollen, soot, ash, smoke, and sea salt — are important because: they act as nuclei of condensation (hygroscopic nuclei) — surfaces around which water vapour condenses to form water droplets, and hence clouds, fog, and precipitation (without such particles, condensation would be much harder); and they scatter, reflect, and absorb incoming sunlight, affecting the colour of the sky (blue sky, and the red/orange colours of sunrise and sunset are due to the scattering of light by these particles and gas molecules). These particles (aerosols) are concentrated in the lower atmosphere. Understanding the role of dust particles (condensation nuclei; scattering light) is a prelims point. Dust particles act as condensation nuclei for cloud formation and scatter sunlight.

stem: The atmosphere is divided into layers on the basis of the vertical variation of:
solution: The atmosphere is divided (vertically) into distinct layers primarily on the basis of the variation of temperature with height (altitude). Because temperature changes with height in different ways in different regions (sometimes decreasing, sometimes increasing), the atmosphere is divided into five main layers — from the surface upward: the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere — each characterised by its own temperature trend. Understanding that atmospheric layers are defined by temperature variation is a prelims point. The atmosphere is divided into layers based on the variation of temperature with height.

stem: The five layers of the atmosphere, in order from the Earth's surface upward, are:
solution: The five main layers of the atmosphere, in order from the Earth's surface upward, are: (1) the troposphere (the lowest layer, where we live and where weather occurs); (2) the stratosphere (containing the ozone layer); (3) the mesosphere (the coldest layer, where meteors burn up); (4) the thermosphere (very hot, containing the ionosphere that reflects radio waves); and (5) the exosphere (the outermost, tenuous layer merging into space). A mnemonic: 'The Small Man Types Exams' (Tropo, Strato, Meso, Thermo, Exo). Understanding the correct order of the atmospheric layers is a prelims point. From the surface up, the layers are: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

stem: The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which we live and in which almost all weather phenomena (clouds, rain, storms) occur, is the:
solution: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere — the layer in contact with the Earth's surface, in which we live and breathe. It is the most important layer for life and weather: almost all the weather phenomena — clouds, rain, snow, fog, storms, thunder, etc. — occur in the troposphere, because this layer contains most of the atmosphere's water vapour, dust, and clouds. In the troposphere, temperature decreases with increasing height (at the 'normal lapse rate'). Understanding the troposphere (the lowest, weather-containing layer) is a key prelims point. The troposphere is the lowest layer, where we live and where weather occurs.

stem: In the troposphere, temperature generally __________ with increasing height.
solution: In the troposphere (the lowest layer of the atmosphere), temperature generally decreases with increasing height (altitude) — that is, it gets colder as you go up. This is because the troposphere is heated mainly from below, by the Earth's surface (which is warmed by the Sun and re-radiates heat), so the air is warmest near the surface and cooler higher up. This normal rate of decrease of temperature with height in the troposphere is called the 'normal lapse rate'. Understanding that temperature decreases with height in the troposphere is a key prelims point. In the troposphere, temperature decreases with increasing height.

stem: The rate at which temperature decreases with increasing height in the troposphere — about 6.5°C per 1000 metres (1 km) — is called the:
solution: The normal lapse rate is the rate at which temperature decreases with increasing height (altitude) in the troposphere, on average about 6.5°C per 1000 metres (1 km) of ascent — i.e., roughly 1°C for every 165 metres. This is why high mountains are cold, and why the top of a tall mountain can have snow even in the tropics. This normal decrease of temperature with height is a standard atmospheric characteristic of the troposphere. Understanding the normal lapse rate (~6.5°C per km) is a prelims point. The normal lapse rate is the fall of temperature with height in the troposphere, about 6.5°C per km.

stem: The average height (thickness) of the troposphere is about:
options: 13 km (about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator)
solution: The average height (thickness) of the troposphere is about 13 km. However, its height is not uniform: it is greater over the equator (about 18 km) and less over the poles (about 8 km). This is because the strong heating and rising (convection) of air over the warm equator pushes the troposphere higher there, while the colder poles have a thinner troposphere. Understanding the troposphere's height (~13 km average; ~18 km at equator, ~8 km at poles) is a prelims point. The troposphere averages about 13 km thick — ~18 km at the equator and ~8 km at the poles.

stem: The upper boundary/limit of the troposphere, above which temperature stops decreasing (a zone of near-constant temperature separating the troposphere from the stratosphere), is called the:
solution: The tropopause is the upper boundary (top) of the troposphere — the transition zone that separates the troposphere below from the stratosphere above. At the tropopause, the fall of temperature with height (which occurs throughout the troposphere) stops, and the temperature becomes almost constant (or the trend reverses). The tropopause is very cold (around −45°C to −80°C, colder over the equator where the troposphere is higher). Understanding the tropopause (the top of the troposphere) is a prelims point. The tropopause is the upper boundary of the troposphere, where the fall of temperature with height stops.

stem: The second layer of the atmosphere, lying just above the troposphere and containing the ozone layer, is the:
solution: The stratosphere is the second layer of the atmosphere, lying just above the troposphere (above the tropopause), extending up to about 50 km. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Because of this absorption of UV radiation by ozone, the stratosphere is warmed from within, so — unlike the troposphere — temperature increases with height in the stratosphere. The stratosphere is largely free of clouds and weather (the air is calm and stable), which is why jet aircraft prefer to fly in the lower stratosphere. Understanding the stratosphere (second layer, contains ozone, calm) is a prelims point. The stratosphere is the second layer, above the troposphere, containing the ozone layer.

stem: In the stratosphere, temperature __________ with increasing height (unlike in the troposphere), mainly because of the absorption of UV radiation by ozone.
solution: In the stratosphere, temperature increases with increasing height — the opposite of the trend in the troposphere (where temperature decreases with height). This temperature increase in the stratosphere is caused mainly by the absorption of the Sun's ultraviolet (UV) radiation by the ozone in the ozone layer: as ozone absorbs UV radiation, it heats the surrounding air, and since ozone (and hence the heating) is more concentrated in the upper stratosphere, the temperature rises with height. Understanding that temperature increases with height in the stratosphere (due to ozone/UV absorption) is a prelims point. In the stratosphere, temperature increases with height because ozone absorbs UV radiation.

stem: Jet aircraft often prefer to fly in the lower stratosphere rather than the troposphere because the stratosphere is:
options: Free of clouds, weather disturbances, and turbulence (calm and stable)
solution: Jet aircraft (and pilots) often prefer to fly in the lower stratosphere (just above the troposphere) because the stratosphere is largely free of clouds, weather disturbances (storms, rain), turbulence, and dust — the air there is calm, stable, and clear (almost all weather is confined to the troposphere below). This makes for a smoother, more comfortable, and more fuel-efficient flight, above the weather. Understanding why aircraft fly in the (lower) stratosphere is a prelims point. Aircraft prefer the stratosphere because it is calm, cloud-free, and free of weather disturbances.

stem: The third layer of the atmosphere, lying above the stratosphere (from about 50 km to 80 km), in which temperature again decreases with height (reaching the lowest temperatures of the atmosphere), is the:
solution: The mesosphere is the third layer of the atmosphere, lying above the stratosphere, extending from about 50 km up to about 80 km. In the mesosphere, temperature decreases with increasing height, reaching the lowest (coldest) temperatures found anywhere in the atmosphere — around −90°C to −100°C at its top (the mesopause). The mesosphere is also the layer in which most meteors (shooting stars) burn up as they enter the atmosphere. Understanding the mesosphere (third layer, coldest, meteors burn) is a prelims point. The mesosphere is the third layer (50–80 km), the coldest, where meteors burn up.

stem: In which atmospheric layer do most meteors (shooting stars) burn up as they enter the Earth's atmosphere?
solution: Most meteors (shooting stars) burn up in the mesosphere — the third layer of the atmosphere (about 50 to 80 km up). As meteoroids (small pieces of rock and debris from space) enter the Earth's atmosphere at very high speed, friction with the air heats them intensely, and most of them burn up (vaporise) in the mesosphere, appearing as the streaks of light we call meteors or shooting stars. Understanding that meteors burn up in the mesosphere is a prelims point. Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere.

stem: The coldest layer of the atmosphere, with the lowest temperatures (around −90°C or lower at its top), is the:
solution: The mesosphere is the coldest layer of the atmosphere. In the mesosphere (about 50–80 km up), temperature decreases with height, reaching its lowest values at the top of the mesosphere (the mesopause), where temperatures fall to around −90°C or lower (some sources cite about −100°C) — the coldest temperatures found anywhere in the Earth's atmosphere. Understanding that the mesosphere is the coldest layer is a prelims point. The mesosphere is the coldest layer of the atmosphere.

stem: The upper boundary of the mesosphere, where the temperature is at its lowest, is called the:
solution: The mesopause is the upper boundary (top) of the mesosphere — the transition zone separating the mesosphere below from the thermosphere above. The mesopause marks the level of the lowest temperature in the atmosphere (around −90°C or lower), because temperature decreases through the mesosphere to reach its minimum here, and then begins to rise again above it (in the thermosphere). (Similarly, the stratopause is the top of the stratosphere, and the tropopause the top of the troposphere.) Understanding the mesopause (the top of the mesosphere, coldest point) is a prelims point. The mesopause is the upper boundary of the mesosphere, marking the coldest point of the atmosphere.

stem: The layer above the mesosphere, in which the ionosphere is located and temperature rises very high with height, is the:
solution: The thermosphere is the layer of the atmosphere above the mesosphere (from about 80 km upward, to roughly several hundred km). In the thermosphere, temperature rises very rapidly and to very high values with increasing height (because the gases here absorb high-energy solar radiation — X-rays and UV) — hence the name 'thermo' (heat). The ionosphere — the electrically charged (ionised) region that reflects radio waves back to Earth (making long-distance radio communication possible) and where auroras occur — is located within the thermosphere. (Note: despite the high 'temperature', the air is so thin that it would not feel hot.) Understanding the thermosphere (contains ionosphere, temperature rises steeply) is a prelims point. The thermosphere lies above the mesosphere, contains the ionosphere, and has temperature rising with height.

stem: The electrically charged (ionised) part of the atmosphere that reflects radio waves back to the Earth (enabling long-distance radio communication) is the:
solution: The ionosphere is the electrically charged (ionised) region of the atmosphere — located within the thermosphere — where the gas molecules are ionised (electrically charged) by the absorption of high-energy solar radiation. The ionosphere is important because it reflects radio waves transmitted from the Earth back down to the Earth's surface, which makes long-distance radio (and wireless) communication possible (the radio waves bounce off the ionosphere and back to distant points on the ground). The beautiful auroras (aurora borealis/australis — the northern and southern lights) also occur in this region. Understanding the ionosphere (reflects radio waves; long-distance communication) is a prelims point. The ionosphere reflects radio waves back to Earth, enabling long-distance radio communication.

stem: The outermost, uppermost layer of the atmosphere, which is extremely thin/rarefied and gradually merges into outer space, is the:
solution: The exosphere is the outermost, uppermost layer of the atmosphere, lying above the thermosphere and extending outward until it gradually merges into outer space (the void of space). In the exosphere, the air is extremely thin and rarefied (very few, widely-spaced gas molecules, mainly light gases like hydrogen and helium), and there is no clear upper boundary — it simply fades away into space. Understanding the exosphere (outermost, thin layer merging into space) is a prelims point. The exosphere is the outermost, extremely thin layer of the atmosphere, merging into space.

stem: Which of the following statements about atmospheric temperature is CORRECT?
options: Temperature increases with height in the troposphere
Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere but increases with height in the stratosphere
Temperature is constant throughout the atmosphere
solution: The correct statement is that temperature decreases with height in the troposphere but increases with height in the stratosphere. In the troposphere (heated from below by the Earth's surface), temperature falls with height (the normal lapse rate). In the stratosphere (where ozone absorbs UV radiation and heats the air), temperature rises with height. (Then in the mesosphere temperature falls again with height, and in the thermosphere it rises again.) So the temperature trend alternates from layer to layer, which is the basis for dividing the atmosphere into layers. Understanding these opposite temperature trends in the troposphere and stratosphere is a prelims point. Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere and increases with height in the stratosphere.

stem: The upper boundary separating the stratosphere from the mesosphere above it is called the:
solution: The stratopause is the upper boundary (top) of the stratosphere — the transition zone that separates the stratosphere below from the mesosphere above (at a height of about 50 km). At the stratopause, the temperature (which had been increasing with height through the stratosphere, due to ozone absorbing UV) reaches a maximum, and above it (in the mesosphere) temperature begins to fall again. (The 'pause' boundaries, from bottom up, are: tropopause, stratopause, mesopause.) Understanding the stratopause (top of the stratosphere) is a prelims point. The stratopause is the upper boundary of the stratosphere.

stem: Together, nitrogen and oxygen make up approximately what percentage of the atmosphere (by volume)?
solution: Together, nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%) make up approximately 99% of the atmosphere by volume. The remaining ~1% consists of argon (~0.93%), carbon dioxide (~0.03%), and other trace gases (neon, helium, ozone, hydrogen, etc.), plus variable amounts of water vapour and dust. So just two gases — nitrogen and oxygen — account for the overwhelming bulk (about 99%) of the air. Understanding that nitrogen + oxygen ≈ 99% of the atmosphere is a prelims point. Nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99% of the atmosphere.

stem: The atmosphere is held to the Earth (prevented from escaping into space) by the force of:
solution: The atmosphere — the envelope of air surrounding the Earth — is held to the Earth, and prevented from escaping into outer space, by the force of the Earth's gravity (gravitational pull). Gravity holds the gases of the atmosphere close to the Earth's surface (which is why the atmosphere is densest near the surface and thins out rapidly with height, and why the vast bulk of the atmosphere lies within a few tens of kilometres of the surface). Understanding that gravity holds the atmosphere is a prelims point. The Earth's gravity holds the atmosphere to the planet.

stem: The density (and pressure) of the atmosphere is greatest __________.
options: At the top of the atmosphere
Near the Earth's surface (in the lower layers), decreasing rapidly with height
solution: The density (and pressure) of the atmosphere is greatest near the Earth's surface (in the lowest layers) and decreases rapidly with increasing height (altitude). This is because gravity pulls the air molecules downward, so they are packed most closely (densest) near the surface, and the air becomes progressively thinner (less dense, lower pressure) as one goes up. In fact, about half of the total mass of the atmosphere lies within the lowest ~5–6 km, and the vast majority within the troposphere. This is why breathing is difficult at high altitudes (thin air). Understanding that atmospheric density/pressure is greatest near the surface and falls with height is a prelims point. Atmospheric density and pressure are greatest near the surface and decrease with height.

stem: The layer of the atmosphere MOST important for living organisms and for weather is the:
solution: The troposphere is the layer of the atmosphere most important for living organisms and for weather. It is the lowest layer, where we (and virtually all life) live and breathe, and it contains most of the atmosphere's mass, water vapour, dust, and clouds. Almost all weather phenomena — clouds, rain, snow, fog, storms, and temperature changes — occur in the troposphere. Because it sustains life and is the seat of weather, the troposphere is the most important layer for humans and biological life. Understanding the special importance of the troposphere is a prelims point. The troposphere is the most important layer for life and weather.

stem: Why is the height of the troposphere greater over the equator than over the poles?
options: The equator is closer to the Sun
Strong heating and vigorous rising (convection) of warm air over the equator pushes the troposphere higher
There is more land at the equator
solution: The height of the troposphere is greater over the equator (about 18 km) than over the poles (about 8 km) mainly because of the strong solar heating at the equator: the intense heating of the equatorial region causes the air to become warm and to rise vigorously (strong convection currents), pushing the top of the troposphere (the tropopause) higher up over the equator. Over the cold poles, there is little heating and rising of air, so the troposphere is thinner (lower). (It is not because the equator is physically 'closer' to the Sun.) Understanding why the troposphere is higher at the equator (strong convection) is a prelims point. The troposphere is higher over the equator because strong heating causes warm air to rise vigorously there.

stem: Which layer contains almost all of the atmosphere's water vapour, clouds, and dust?
solution: The troposphere (the lowest layer of the atmosphere) contains almost all of the atmosphere's water vapour, clouds, and dust particles. This is why virtually all weather phenomena (clouds, rain, fog, storms) occur in the troposphere, and why the stratosphere above it is clear and free of weather. The concentration of moisture and dust in the troposphere, together with its being heated from below, makes it the dynamic, weather-producing layer. Understanding that the troposphere holds almost all the water vapour, clouds, and dust is a prelims point. The troposphere contains almost all of the atmosphere's water vapour, clouds, and dust.

stem: The gases that maintain fairly constant proportions up to about 90 km (making the lower atmosphere well-mixed and uniform in composition) constitute the region called the:
solution: The homosphere is the lower region of the atmosphere (roughly up to about 90 km), in which the atmospheric gases are well mixed and maintain fairly constant, uniform proportions (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, etc. in nearly the same ratios throughout) — because turbulence and mixing keep the gases evenly blended ('homo' = same). Above it lies the heterosphere, where the gases are no longer uniformly mixed but tend to separate into layers by weight (lighter gases higher up). Understanding the homosphere (well-mixed lower atmosphere of uniform composition) is a prelims point. The homosphere is the lower, well-mixed region of uniform gas composition (up to ~90 km).

stem: Above about 90 km, the atmosphere is called the heterosphere, where the gases:
options: Are no longer well mixed but tend to separate into layers according to their weight (lighter gases higher up)
solution: The heterosphere is the region of the atmosphere above about 90 km, where the gases are no longer well mixed (uniform) as in the homosphere below, but instead tend to separate/stratify into layers according to their molecular weight — with the heavier gases (like oxygen and nitrogen) lower down and the lighter gases (like helium and hydrogen) at the top ('hetero' = different). This separation occurs because, at these great heights, the air is so thin that mixing (turbulence) is weak, and gravity sorts the gases by weight. Understanding the heterosphere (gases layered by weight above ~90 km) is a prelims point. In the heterosphere (above ~90 km), gases separate into layers by weight, lighter gases rising highest.

stem: The blue colour of the daytime sky is mainly caused by the:
options: Scattering of sunlight (especially blue light) by the gas molecules and fine particles of the atmosphere
solution: The blue colour of the daytime sky is mainly caused by the scattering of sunlight by the gas molecules (and fine dust particles) of the atmosphere. Sunlight (white light) is made up of all colours; as it passes through the atmosphere, the shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered (deflected in all directions) much more strongly than the longer-wavelength red light — so the scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all over the sky, making the sky appear blue. (The same scattering process — with red/orange light dominating when sunlight travels a long, low path through the atmosphere — causes the reddish colours of sunrise and sunset.) Understanding that atmospheric scattering causes the blue sky is a prelims point. The blue sky results from the scattering of (blue) sunlight by atmospheric molecules and particles.

stem: The 'greenhouse gases' in the atmosphere (such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, and methane) are important because they:
options: Cool the Earth by blocking all sunlight
Trap/absorb outgoing heat (terrestrial radiation) and keep the Earth warm enough to support life (the greenhouse effect)
solution: Greenhouse gases — such as carbon dioxide (CO2), water vapour, methane (CH4), and others — are important because they trap and absorb the outgoing heat (long-wave terrestrial/infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface) and re-radiate part of it back downward, thereby keeping the lower atmosphere and the Earth's surface warmer than they would otherwise be. This natural 'greenhouse effect' keeps the Earth warm enough (with a habitable average temperature) to support life. However, the increase of greenhouse gases (especially CO2) due to human activities is intensifying this effect, causing global warming and climate change. Understanding the greenhouse effect (greenhouse gases trap heat, warming the Earth) is a prelims point. Greenhouse gases trap outgoing heat, keeping the Earth warm (the greenhouse effect).

stem: The depletion (thinning) of the ozone layer — for example the 'ozone hole' over Antarctica — is a concern because a thinner ozone layer allows more __________ to reach the Earth's surface.
solution: The depletion (thinning) of the ozone layer — including the 'ozone hole' observed over Antarctica — is a serious concern because the ozone layer normally absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation; when the ozone layer is thinned/depleted, more of this harmful UV radiation is able to reach the Earth's surface. Increased UV radiation can cause skin cancer, cataracts and eye damage, weakening of the immune system, and harm to plants, crops, and marine life (plankton). Ozone depletion has been caused mainly by human-made chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Understanding that ozone depletion lets more harmful UV reach the surface is a prelims point. Ozone depletion allows more harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation to reach the Earth's surface.

stem: The atmosphere is essential for life on Earth because it:
options: Provides gases for breathing (oxygen) and photosynthesis (CO2), shields us from harmful radiation and meteors, and moderates temperature
solution: The atmosphere is essential for life on Earth for many reasons: it provides the gases needed by living things — oxygen for respiration (breathing) and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis by plants; it shields life from harmful solar radiation (the ozone layer absorbs harmful UV rays) and from meteors (which mostly burn up in the mesosphere); it moderates the Earth's temperature (the greenhouse effect keeps the planet warm, and the atmosphere prevents extreme heating by day and extreme cooling by night); and it is the medium of weather and the water cycle (bringing rainfall). Without the atmosphere, life as we know it could not exist. Understanding why the atmosphere is essential for life is a prelims point. The atmosphere provides breathable/photosynthetic gases, shields us from radiation and meteors, and moderates temperature.

stem: Which gas is a raw material for photosynthesis (used by green plants to make food), and is also breathed out by animals?
solution: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gas that green plants use as a raw material in photosynthesis — the process by which plants, using sunlight, combine CO2 and water to make their food (glucose) and release oxygen. Carbon dioxide is also the gas breathed out (exhaled) by animals (and humans) during respiration, and it is released by the burning of fuels. Thus CO2 links animal respiration/combustion (which release it) with plant photosynthesis (which uses it) in the carbon cycle. Understanding CO2's role in photosynthesis is a prelims point. Carbon dioxide is used by plants in photosynthesis and is breathed out by animals.

stem: Concentration of carbon dioxide and water vapour is confined mainly to the __________ of the atmosphere.
solution: The concentration of carbon dioxide and water vapour is confined mainly to the lower layers of the atmosphere — that is, close to the Earth's surface (largely within the troposphere). Carbon dioxide is found mostly in the lower atmosphere (its concentration decreasing with height), and water vapour, which comes from evaporation at the surface, is also concentrated in the lowest layers and decreases rapidly with height. Because these greenhouse gases (and the dust and clouds) are concentrated in the lower atmosphere, that is where the greenhouse warming and weather are focused. Understanding that CO2 and water vapour are concentrated in the lower atmosphere is a prelims point. Carbon dioxide and water vapour are concentrated mainly in the lower atmosphere.

stem: The layer in which auroras (the northern and southern lights, aurora borealis/australis) occur is the:
solution: Auroras — the beautiful, glowing light displays known as the aurora borealis (northern lights) and aurora australis (southern lights) — occur in the thermosphere, specifically within the ionosphere (the ionised region of the thermosphere), at high latitudes near the poles. Auroras are produced when charged particles from the Sun (the solar wind) enter the upper atmosphere and interact with (excite) the gas molecules there, causing them to emit light. Understanding that auroras occur in the thermosphere/ionosphere is a prelims point. Auroras occur in the thermosphere (in the ionosphere).

stem: Which of the following correctly lists a layer with its key feature?
solution: The correct pairing is: Stratosphere — contains the ozone layer. Each layer has its own key feature: the troposphere is where weather occurs and where we live; the stratosphere contains the ozone layer (which absorbs UV radiation); the mesosphere is the coldest layer, where meteors burn up; the thermosphere contains the ionosphere (which reflects radio waves) and where auroras occur; and the exosphere is the outermost layer, merging into space. (So 'troposphere — contains ozone', 'mesosphere — reflects radio waves', and 'exosphere — where weather occurs' are all incorrect.) Understanding the correct layer-feature matching is a prelims point. The stratosphere contains the ozone layer.

stem: Assertion (A): The stratosphere is an ideal layer for flying jet aircraft. Reason (R): The stratosphere is generally free of clouds and weather-related turbulence. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the stratosphere (its lower part) is an ideal layer for flying jet aircraft. And this is precisely because (R) the stratosphere is generally free of clouds, water vapour, dust, and weather-related turbulence — the air there is calm, stable, and clear (almost all weather being confined to the troposphere below). This calm, cloud-free condition is exactly why the stratosphere is ideal for aircraft (smoother, more efficient flight above the weather). So R is the correct explanation of A. Understanding this cause-and-effect (calm stratosphere → good for aircraft) is a prelims point. The stratosphere is ideal for aircraft because it is free of clouds and turbulence.

stem: Which of the following gases is NOT one of the two most abundant gases in the atmosphere?
options: Both nitrogen and oxygen are the two most abundant
solution: Carbon dioxide is NOT one of the two most abundant gases in the atmosphere. The two most abundant gases are nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%), which together make up about 99% of the air. Carbon dioxide, despite its climatic importance, makes up only about 0.03% of the atmosphere — a tiny fraction — so it is not among the most abundant gases. Understanding that CO2 is a trace gas (not among the two most abundant) is a prelims point. Carbon dioxide (~0.03%) is not one of the two most abundant gases; nitrogen and oxygen are.

stem: In which layer would you experience the phenomenon of 'weather' (clouds, rain, wind, storms)?
solution: You would experience 'weather' — clouds, rain, snow, wind, thunderstorms, fog, and changing temperatures — in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere. This is because the troposphere contains almost all of the atmosphere's water vapour, dust, and clouds, and it is heated from below by the Earth's surface (setting up the convection and instability that drive weather). The layers above the troposphere (stratosphere and higher) are essentially free of weather. Understanding that all weather occurs in the troposphere is a key prelims point. Weather (clouds, rain, storms) occurs in the troposphere.

stem: The variable gases and components of the atmosphere (whose amounts change from place to place and time to time) include:
options: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, and dust particles
solution: The variable components of the atmosphere — those whose amounts change (vary) considerably from place to place and time to time — include water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, and dust particles. Water vapour is highly variable (from near 0% over deserts/poles to ~4% over warm oceans); carbon dioxide and ozone also vary; and dust particles vary depending on location (more over dry, dusty, or polluted areas). In contrast, the permanent (fixed) gases — nitrogen, oxygen, and argon — maintain nearly constant proportions throughout the lower atmosphere. Understanding which components are variable is a prelims point. Water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, and dust are the variable components of the atmosphere.

stem: Which layer of the atmosphere lies immediately ABOVE the troposphere?
solution: The stratosphere lies immediately above the troposphere (separated from it by the tropopause). The order of layers from the surface upward is: troposphere → stratosphere → mesosphere → thermosphere → exosphere. So directly above the troposphere is the stratosphere (which contains the ozone layer). Understanding the sequence of layers — and that the stratosphere sits just above the troposphere — is a prelims point. The stratosphere lies immediately above the troposphere.

stem: The gas that makes up the largest proportion (about 78%) of the atmosphere is:
solution: Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the atmosphere by volume, making it the most abundant gas in the air.

stem: Oxygen makes up approximately what proportion of the atmosphere?
solution: Oxygen makes up about 21 per cent of the atmosphere by volume, the second most abundant gas after nitrogen and essential for the respiration of living organisms.

stem: After nitrogen and oxygen, the next most abundant gas in the atmosphere is:
solution: Argon, making up about 0.93 per cent of the atmosphere, is the third most abundant gas after nitrogen and oxygen.

stem: Carbon dioxide makes up only about __________ of the atmosphere.
solution: Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.03-0.04 per cent of the atmosphere, but it is very important as a greenhouse gas and a raw material for photosynthesis.

stem: The 'ozone layer', which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, is found in the:
solution: The ozone layer is located in the stratosphere (roughly 15-35 km altitude); it absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, protecting life on Earth.

stem: The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which we live and where most weather occurs, is the:
solution: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, containing most of its mass, water vapour and dust; it is where almost all weather phenomena occur.

stem: In the troposphere, temperature generally __________ with increasing altitude.
solution: In the troposphere, temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude, at an average rate called the normal lapse rate.

stem: The rate at which temperature decreases with height in the troposphere (about 6.5 C per 1000 m) is called the:
solution: The normal lapse rate is the average rate at which temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere — about 6.5 degrees Celsius per 1000 metres.

stem: The upper boundary of the troposphere, above which temperature stops decreasing, is called the:
solution: The tropopause is the upper boundary of the troposphere, separating it from the stratosphere; above it, temperature stops decreasing with height.

stem: In the stratosphere, temperature __________ with increasing altitude.
solution: In the stratosphere, temperature increases with altitude, because the ozone layer there absorbs ultraviolet radiation and warms the upper part of this layer.

stem: Jet aircraft often prefer to fly in the lower stratosphere because it:
options: Is stable, cloud-free and free of turbulence and weather
solution: The lower stratosphere is ideal for flying jet aircraft because it is stable, largely cloud-free, and free of the turbulence and weather disturbances that occur in the troposphere below.

stem: In which atmospheric layer do most meteors (shooting stars) burn up?
solution: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, the layer above the stratosphere, due to friction with the air as they fall towards the Earth.

stem: The coldest layer of the atmosphere, with the lowest temperatures, is the:
solution: The mesosphere is the coldest layer of the atmosphere; temperature decreases with height in it, reaching the lowest values (around -90 C) at its upper boundary, the mesopause.

stem: The electrically charged (ionised) part of the atmosphere that reflects radio waves back to Earth is the:
solution: The ionosphere, located in the thermosphere, contains electrically charged (ionised) particles; it reflects radio waves back to the Earth, making long-distance radio communication possible.

stem: Assertion (A): The stratosphere is an ideal layer for flying jet aircraft. Reason (R): It is stable and largely free from clouds, turbulence and weather disturbances.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The stratosphere is ideal for jet flight because its stability and lack of clouds, turbulence and weather make for a smooth flight — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The ozone layer is vital for life on Earth. Reason (R): It absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The ozone layer is vital because it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, protecting living organisms from its damaging effects — R explains A.

stem: The five layers of the atmosphere, in order upward from the Earth's surface, are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and:
solution: The five layers of the atmosphere, from the surface upward, are: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere (the outermost layer).

stem: The outermost, uppermost layer of the atmosphere, which gradually merges into outer space, is the:
solution: The exosphere is the outermost layer of the atmosphere, extremely rarefied, gradually merging with outer space; its gases slowly escape into space.

stem: Water vapour in the atmosphere is important because it:
options: Contributes to weather (clouds, rain) and absorbs heat (a greenhouse gas)
solution: Water vapour is important because it is the source of all precipitation (clouds, rain, snow), it absorbs and releases heat (acting as a greenhouse gas), and it influences weather and climate.

stem: Tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere (dust, pollen, soot, salt) are important because they:
options: Act as nuclei for cloud formation and scatter sunlight
solution: Solid particles (aerosols) in the atmosphere are important because they act as nuclei (hygroscopic particles) around which water vapour condenses to form clouds, and they scatter sunlight, affecting sky colour and temperature.

stem: Match the layer with its feature: (i) Troposphere (ii) Stratosphere (iii) Mesosphere — (a) ozone layer (b) coldest, meteors burn up (c) weather occurs:
solution: The troposphere is where weather occurs, the stratosphere contains the ozone layer, and the mesosphere is the coldest layer where meteors burn up.

stem: The layer of the atmosphere above the mesosphere, where temperature rises sharply and the ionosphere lies, is the:
solution: The thermosphere lies above the mesosphere; temperature rises sharply with height in it, and it contains the ionosphere, which reflects radio waves.

stem: The 'greenhouse gases' in the atmosphere (such as carbon dioxide and water vapour) are important because they:
options: Trap heat and keep the Earth warm enough for life
solution: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane trap outgoing heat (long-wave radiation) in the atmosphere, keeping the Earth warm enough to support life; too much of them causes global warming.

stem: The depletion (thinning) of the ozone layer is a concern because it:
options: Allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation to reach the Earth's surface
solution: The depletion of the ozone layer (e.g. the ozone hole over Antarctica), caused by pollutants like CFCs, is a serious concern because it allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation to reach the surface, harming living organisms.

stem: The density (and pressure) of the atmosphere is greatest:
options: At the top of the atmosphere
solution: The density and pressure of the atmosphere are greatest near the Earth's surface, where the air is compressed by the weight of the air above, and both decrease rapidly with increasing altitude.

stem: Carbon dioxide is important as a raw material for __________ carried out by green plants.
solution: Carbon dioxide is the raw material used by green plants in photosynthesis (along with water and sunlight) to produce food and release oxygen, making it essential for life.

stem: The concentration of carbon dioxide and water vapour in the atmosphere is confined mainly to the:
solution: Carbon dioxide and water vapour are concentrated mainly in the lower layers of the atmosphere (the troposphere), which is why weather and the greenhouse effect occur there.

stem: The atmosphere is divided into layers mainly on the basis of:
solution: The atmosphere is divided into layers (troposphere, stratosphere, etc.) mainly on the basis of the way temperature changes with increasing altitude in each layer.

stem: The height of the troposphere is greater over the equator than over the poles because:
options: Strong convection currents at the equator push the troposphere higher
There is no air at the equator
solution: The troposphere is thicker over the equator (about 18 km) than over the poles (about 8 km) because strong heating and convection currents at the equator push the troposphere to greater heights.

stem: The layer of the atmosphere in which the auroras (northern and southern lights) occur is the:
solution: The auroras (northern and southern lights) occur in the thermosphere (in the ionosphere region), where charged particles from the Sun interact with atmospheric gases, producing glowing lights.

stem: The gases nitrogen and oxygen together make up approximately what percentage of the atmosphere?
solution: Nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%) together make up approximately 99 per cent of the atmosphere by volume, with all other gases forming the remaining 1 per cent.

stem: Which layer would you find immediately ABOVE the stratosphere?
solution: The mesosphere lies immediately above the stratosphere; the order upward is troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere.

stem: The upper boundary of the stratosphere, separating it from the mesosphere, is called the:
solution: The stratopause is the upper boundary of the stratosphere, separating it from the mesosphere above.

stem: The composition of the atmosphere is fairly uniform (well-mixed) up to a height of about 90 km, a region called the:
solution: Up to about 90 km, the gases of the atmosphere are well-mixed in fairly constant proportions, a region called the homosphere; above it, in the heterosphere, gases separate into layers by weight.

stem: Which of the following gases, though present in tiny amounts, is important for protecting life from ultraviolet radiation?
solution: Ozone, though present in only tiny amounts (mainly in the stratosphere), is very important because it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, protecting life on Earth.

stem: The variable gases and components of the atmosphere (whose amounts change from place to place) include water vapour, dust and:
solution: The variable components of the atmosphere, whose proportions change with place and time, include water vapour, dust particles, and gases like ozone and carbon dioxide, unlike the fairly constant nitrogen and oxygen.

stem: The layer of the atmosphere most important for living organisms and weather is the:
solution: The troposphere is the most important layer for living organisms and weather, as it contains most of the atmosphere's air, water vapour and dust, and is where clouds, rain and other weather occur.

stem: Above about 90 km, the atmosphere is called the heterosphere because:
options: The gases separate into layers according to their weight
solution: Above about 90 km, in the heterosphere, the gases are no longer well-mixed but tend to separate into layers according to their molecular weight, with lighter gases at the top.

stem: In the exosphere, one would experience the phenomenon of the atmosphere:
options: Gradually merging into the near-vacuum of outer space
solution: In the exosphere, the outermost layer, the atmosphere is extremely thin and gradually merges into the near-vacuum of outer space, with gas molecules so sparse that some escape into space.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Composition and Structure of Atmosphere' is that:
options: The atmosphere is a layered mixture of gases essential for life and weather
solution: The chapter concludes that the atmosphere is a layered envelope of gases (mainly nitrogen and oxygen), water vapour and particles, structured into distinct layers by temperature, and that it is essential for life, weather and the protection of the Earth.
